title: Network Layer Overview: Forwarding, Routing, Planes, Service Models

questions.q: At the sending host, what does the network layer do with a segment it receives from the transport layer?
choices: Encapsulates it into a datagram and passes the datagram to the link layer
Delivers it to the transport-layer protocol of the receiving process
Passes the segment's bits directly to the physical layer, skipping the link layer
Examines its header fields to choose a router output port
questions.explain: The sender's network layer wraps (encapsulates) the transport segment in a datagram and hands it down to the link layer. Delivering segments up to the transport layer is what the receiver does.

questions.q: At the receiving host, what is the network layer's job?
choices: Encapsulate the segment into a new datagram for the next hop
Deliver the segment up to the transport-layer protocol
Compute the route back to the sender
Move the datagram from an input port to an output port
questions.explain: The network layer carries segments from the sending host to the receiving host. At the receiver it delivers the segment up to the transport-layer protocol.

questions.q: Network-layer protocols run only in end hosts. Routers handle datagrams purely at the link layer.
questions.explain: Network-layer protocols run in every Internet device, both hosts and routers. A router's main job is network-layer work: it examines IP datagram headers and forwards the datagrams.

questions.q: Which layers of the protocol stack does a router in the middle of an end-to-end path implement?
choices: Application
Transport
Network
Link
Physical
questions.explain: End hosts implement all five layers. Routers along the path implement only the network, link and physical layers, which is enough to examine IP headers and forward datagrams.

questions.q: Which IP datagrams does a router examine the header fields of?
choices: All IP datagrams passing through it
Only the first datagram of each connection
Only datagrams addressed to the router itself
Only datagrams that arrive out of order
questions.explain: A router examines the header fields of every IP datagram passing through it, then moves the datagram from an input port to an output port along the end-to-end path.

questions.q: What is the name of the network-layer packet that carries a transport-layer segment from the sending host to the receiving host?
questions.explain: The sender encapsulates segments into datagrams. In the Internet these are IP datagrams.

questions.q: Which description matches forwarding?
choices: Moving packets from a router's input link to the appropriate router output link
Determining the route packets take from source to destination
Running routing algorithms to plan end-to-end paths
Delivering segments up to the transport layer at the receiver
questions.explain: Forwarding is the per-router step of moving a packet from an input link to the right output link. Determining the whole source-to-destination route, using routing algorithms, is routing.

questions.q: In the 'taking a trip' analogy, which pairing is correct?
choices: Forwarding = getting through a single interchange; routing = planning the trip from source to destination
Forwarding = planning the trip from source to destination; routing = getting through a single interchange
Forwarding and routing both = getting through a single interchange
Forwarding and routing both = planning the trip from source to destination
questions.explain: Forwarding is local, like getting through one highway interchange. Routing is global, like planning the whole route on a map from source to destination.

questions.q: Something in the network works out that datagrams from host A to host B should travel through routers R1, R3 and R4. Which network-layer function is this, and what carries it out?
choices: Routing, carried out by routing algorithms
Forwarding, carried out by a single router's forwarding table
Forwarding, carried out by routing algorithms
Encapsulation, carried out by the sending host
questions.explain: Determining the route packets take from source to destination is routing, and routing algorithms carry it out. Forwarding only moves a packet from one router's input link to an output link.

questions.q: A router's local forwarding table maps header values to output ports: 0100 → port 3, 0110 → port 2, 0111 → port 2, 1001 → port 1. A datagram arrives with header value 0100. Which output port is it forwarded to?
questions.explain: Forwarding means looking up the value from the arriving packet's header in the local forwarding table. The entry for 0100 says output port 3.

questions.q: In a router's forwarding table, each output port can appear for at most one header value.
questions.explain: Several header values can map to the same output port. For example, a table can send both 0110 and 0111 to port 2.

questions.q: Forwarding concerns the whole end-to-end path, while routing concerns what happens inside a single router.
questions.explain: It's the other way around. Forwarding is the per-router input-link-to-output-link step. Routing determines the end-to-end route from source to destination.

questions.q: Which describes the data plane?
choices: A local, per-router function that determines how a datagram arriving on an input port is forwarded to an output port
Network-wide logic that determines how a datagram is routed among routers along the end-end path
A remote controller that computes forwarding tables for all routers
Replicated application-layer services placed close to clients
questions.explain: The data plane is local and per-router: it uses values in the arriving packet's header to pick the output port. Network-wide routing logic belongs to the control plane.

questions.q: The control plane is network-wide logic that determines how a datagram is routed among routers along the end-end path from source host to destination host.
questions.explain: Control plane = network-wide logic for routing among routers. Data plane = the local, per-router forwarding function.

questions.q: Which of these are data-plane activities?
choices: A router reads a value in an arriving packet's header and looks it up to choose an output port
Routing-algorithm components in different routers exchange information to compute paths
A remote controller computes forwarding tables and installs them in routers
A router moves a datagram from its input port to the chosen output port
questions.explain: Looking up the header value and moving the datagram to an output port are local, per-router forwarding, which is the data plane. Computing paths or tables, whether by routers working together or by a remote controller, is the control plane.

questions.q: In the traditional (per-router) control-plane approach, where are routing algorithms implemented?
choices: In each and every router, with the routing components in different routers interacting with each other
In a single remote controller that installs forwarding tables in routers
Only in the end hosts at either end of the path
In the link layer of each router
questions.explain: In a per-router control plane, every router runs its own routing-algorithm component. These components interact with each other, and each router's component fills in that router's local forwarding table.

questions.q: In software-defined networking (SDN), what computes the forwarding tables and installs them in routers?
choices: A remote controller running on (remote) servers
A routing algorithm running inside each router
The network layer of the sending host
The link layer of the next-hop router
questions.explain: With SDN, the control plane is implemented in remote servers: a remote controller computes forwarding tables and installs them in the routers.

questions.q: In an SDN control plane, each router still runs its own full routing algorithm and exchanges routing information directly with other routers.
questions.explain: In SDN, routers don't compute routes among themselves. Each router has an agent (CA) that interacts with the remote controller, and the controller computes the tables and installs them.

questions.q: Under both the traditional per-router control plane and the SDN control plane, each router still uses its own local forwarding table to forward arriving datagrams.
questions.explain: The two approaches differ only in how the forwarding tables get computed: by routing algorithms in every router, or by a remote controller. Either way, each router's data plane forwards packets by looking them up in its local table.

questions.q: Which of these are example services for a flow of datagrams, as opposed to services for individual datagrams?
choices: In-order datagram delivery
Guaranteed minimum bandwidth to the flow
Restrictions on changes in inter-packet spacing
Guaranteed delivery
Guaranteed delivery with less than 40 msec delay
questions.explain: Order, bandwidth to a flow, and inter-packet spacing only make sense across a sequence of datagrams, so they are flow services. Guaranteed delivery, with or without a delay bound, can apply to a single datagram.

questions.q: Why is in-order delivery a service for a flow of datagrams rather than for an individual datagram?
choices: Order only has meaning relative to the other datagrams in the same flow
Individual datagrams have no header fields
In-order delivery can only be provided by an SDN controller
Individual datagrams are always delivered in order automatically
questions.explain: A single datagram has no order by itself. Ordering, like minimum bandwidth or inter-packet spacing, describes how a sequence (flow) of datagrams is treated.

questions.q: Network service models are compared on their QoS guarantees (bandwidth, loss, order, timing). What does QoS stand for?
questions.explain: QoS = Quality of Service: what a service model guarantees about bandwidth, loss, order and timing.

questions.q: What does ATM's Constant Bit Rate (CBR) service model guarantee?
choices: Constant-rate bandwidth, plus guarantees on loss, order and timing
A guaranteed minimum bandwidth and in-order delivery, but no loss or timing guarantee
No bandwidth, loss, order or timing guarantees at all
Possibly bandwidth, loss and order guarantees, but no timing guarantee
questions.explain: ATM CBR: constant-rate bandwidth, and yes to loss, order and timing. The other choices describe ATM ABR, Internet best effort and Diffserv.

questions.q: Which service model guarantees a minimum bandwidth and in-order delivery, but no loss or timing?
choices: ATM Available Bit Rate (ABR)
ATM Constant Bit Rate (CBR)
Intserv Guaranteed
Internet best effort
questions.explain: ATM ABR: bandwidth = guaranteed minimum, loss = no, order = yes, timing = no.

questions.q: Which Internet service model offers guarantees on all four of bandwidth, loss, order and timing?
choices: Intserv Guaranteed (RFC 1633)
Diffserv (RFC 2475)
Best effort
None: no Internet service model can guarantee timing
questions.explain: Intserv Guaranteed (RFC 1633) answers yes for bandwidth, loss, order and timing. Diffserv offers only 'possible/possibly' and no timing. Best effort guarantees nothing.

questions.q: Diffserv (RFC 2475) provides a timing guarantee.
questions.explain: Diffserv: bandwidth possible, loss possibly, order possibly, timing no.

questions.q: Which of these service models guarantee timing?
choices: Internet best effort
ATM Constant Bit Rate
ATM Available Bit Rate
Intserv Guaranteed
Diffserv
questions.explain: Only ATM CBR and Intserv Guaranteed say yes for timing. Best effort, ATM ABR and Diffserv say no.

questions.q: A host sends datagrams 1, 2 and 3 to another host over the Internet's network layer. Which outcome does the best-effort service model rule out?
choices: They arrive in the order 3, 1, 2
Datagram 2 never arrives
All three arrive, but with very different delays
None of these: best effort rules out none of them
questions.explain: Best effort guarantees nothing about successful delivery, timing or order of delivery, or bandwidth for an end-end flow. So reordering, loss and variable delay are all possible.

questions.q: The Internet's best-effort service model guarantees a minimum amount of bandwidth to each end-end flow.
questions.explain: Best effort's bandwidth guarantee is 'none'. It offers no guarantee on the bandwidth available to an end-end flow, and no guarantees on loss, order or timing either.

questions.q: Which of these help explain why the best-effort service model works well in practice?
choices: Its simple mechanism let the Internet be widely deployed and adopted
Enough bandwidth provisioning makes real-time applications 'good enough' most of the time
Replicated application-layer services (datacenters, CDNs) connect close to clients' networks
Congestion control of 'elastic' services
Every router reserves a guaranteed bandwidth for each flow
The network layer guarantees delivery of every datagram
questions.explain: Simplicity, bandwidth provisioning, replicated application-layer services close to clients, and congestion control of elastic services all help. Per-flow reservations and guaranteed delivery are exactly what best effort does NOT provide.

questions.q: With no timing or bandwidth guarantees, what lets real-time applications such as interactive voice and video work acceptably over best-effort service?
choices: Sufficient provisioning of bandwidth, so performance is 'good enough' most of the time
The network layer reserving a fixed bit rate for each call
Routers guaranteeing delivery in under 40 msec
Forwarding tables that prioritize voice packets by default
questions.explain: Enough bandwidth provisioning makes real-time applications 'good enough' most of the time, even though best effort itself guarantees nothing.

questions.q: How do replicated, application-layer distributed services such as datacenters and content distribution networks make up for the lack of network-layer guarantees?
choices: They connect close to clients' networks, so services can be provided from multiple locations
They add delivery and timing guarantees to the IP layer
They replace routers' forwarding tables with their own
They make the network layer deliver datagrams in order
questions.explain: Putting replicated services near clients' networks means content can come from multiple nearby locations. This improves service at the application layer without changing the best-effort network layer.
